analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run public health insurance plan sold alongside private plans on the ACA exchanges.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Health Committee at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The CHOICE Act would direct the federal government to offer its own silver, gold, and bronze health plans on the ACA marketplaces starting in 2023. The government plan would follow the same rules as private plans, set premiums by region, and negotiate prices with doctors, hospitals, and drug makers — falling back to standard Medicare payment rates if no deal is reached. Doctors and hospitals already in Medicare or Medicaid would be in the network automatically unless they opt out. Its backers pitched it as a cheaper competitor that would pressure private insurers to lower prices.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy coverage on the ACA exchanges — individuals, families, and small-business employees without employer insurance — would get a new, likely cheaper government option. The bill requires the plan to meet all the same consumer protections and benefit rules as private plans [S2] [S3], and its administrative costs are designed to be lean, with premiums set to cover only the cost of care and operations [S3]. People in areas with few insurers or high premiums would have an alternative backed by the government's bargaining power.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People buying coverage on ACA exchanges

how_it_helps.text: Creates a public health insurance option sold on the exchanges, offering silver and gold plans (and optionally bronze) with all essential benefits, consumer protections, and cost-sharing limits that apply to private marketplace plans [S2] [S3].

Directs the government to negotiate provider and prescription drug payment rates, falling back to standard Medicare rates if no agreement is reached — rates that are typically well below what private insurers pay [S2] [S3].
Makes every Medicare and Medicaid provider part of the network automatically unless they opt out, so enrollees would have broad access to doctors and hospitals from day one [S2] [S3].
Requires premiums to be geographically adjusted and set only high enough to cover benefits and administration, and bars states from taxing the plan's funds, keeping overhead low [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would face direct competition on their home turf for the first time, with a government plan whose lower overhead and Medicare-level payment rates could undercut their premiums. Hospitals and doctors would be paid Medicare-level rates by the public plan for patients they accept, below the higher private-insurer rates. Drug makers would face a large new payer negotiating prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private insurers, hospitals, and drug makers

drawbacks.text: The plan must be financed entirely by its own premiums with a contingency margin, with no ongoing taxpayer subsidy beyond start-up funding that must be repaid over ten years — so if enrollment is small or costs run high, premiums could end up less affordable than promised [S3].

Falling back to Medicare fee-for-service payment rates for providers and drugs could push some hospitals and physicians to opt out of the network, shrinking access for enrollees in areas with thin provider participation [S3].

Opponents of a public option argue a government plan backed by Medicare's low payment rates and start-up funding has structural advantages private plans cannot match, and could eventually crowd private coverage out of the market rather than compete with it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 30 million uninsured Americans and millions more paying full price for marketplace coverage, a Medicare-style option with broad provider access and negotiated rates is a substantial potential benefit, and the bill is written to be self-financing rather than a new open-ended entitlement. The main costs fall on insurers, hospitals, and drug makers through lower revenues and tighter rates; the main risk to the public is that the plan underpays providers, leading some to opt out and limiting where enrollees can get care.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on March 25, 2021, with Sen. Sherrod Brown as the bill's cosponsor [S1] [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed for the rest of the 117th Congress [S5].
The bill drew just one cosponsor, Sen. Sherrod Brown, and never advanced beyond referral [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers keep the ACA exchange market to themselves with no government-run competitor, and hospitals and drug makers avoid Medicare-level payment rates on the exchanges.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private health insurers and large providers

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the CHOICE Act to create a public health insurance option on the ACA exchanges

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and no Republican supported the bill; it never advanced far enough for a recorded party split.

industries.note: A government plan sold on the same exchanges, with lower overhead and Medicare-level payment rates, would compete directly for their customers and could push premiums down market-wide. Insurers' interest in keeping the public option off the table runs against people looking for cheaper coverage.

They would gain millions of potential new covered patients through automatic network participation, but be paid at Medicare rates — typically well below private insurer rates — unless they opt out. Their incentive to block or opt out comes from accepting lower payments that would otherwise be charged to patients as higher premiums.

The public plan would negotiate drug payment rates, falling back to Medicare fee-for-service rates — a new large payer bargaining prices down. Lower drug prices under the plan would mean lower premiums for enrollees.
CMS may contract with third parties to administer the public option's operations, creating new business for firms that already run Medicare administrative functions.
